titulo.texto: Altar of Mictlantecuhtli from El Zapotal (replica)

frase_gancho.texto: The lord of death, made of raw clay, seated on his throne.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the lord of death in the hall’s garden, we return to the display cases and to an Olmec tomb. Look for a small seated figure of green stone, barely eight centimeters tall, with a polished disc gleaming on its chest.

guion_corto.texto: This seated figure is the lord of death. What you see in the hall’s garden is a replica: the original is in El Zapotal, in central Veracruz, and it was modeled from raw, unfired clay and then painted. It is so fragile that it had to stay at the site, where there is now a museum. Look at the body, very thin, almost skeletal, and at the headdress, which bears human skulls. We call him Mictlantecuhtli, a Nahuatl name that means “lord of Mictlán,” the place of the dead. But this altar is several centuries older than the Mexica, and we do not know what the people who made it called him.

guion_largo.texto:
This piece has a catch, and it is best to say so right away: what you see is a replica. The original Mictlantecuhtli was modeled from unfired clay, and that material, after more than a thousand years, is among the most fragile there is. That is why it stayed in El Zapotal, where a museum was built to protect it, and here we see a copy. Even so, it is worth pausing, because it is one of the most striking images of death made by the ancient peoples of Mexico.

Let us begin with the site. El Zapotal is in central Veracruz, and it was inhabited between the years six hundred and nine hundred of our era, in the heart of the Classic period. It became known in 1971, when burials appeared with offerings of clay figures. The [Cihuateteo](mna_s08_cihuateteo_zapotal) you saw in this very hall comes from the same place, and it is thought to have been part of a sanctuary dedicated to death. This altar is the heart of that sanctuary.

Now, the face of death. The figure is seated on a throne, with an extremely thin body, almost a skeleton, and in its headdress it wears human skulls. There is nothing of a children’s story about it: this is death seen head-on, with no adornments to soften it. And yet, it is not alone on its throne: it is a character with a court and a name, like a ruler. In Mesoamerica, death was not nothingness, but a place with a lord.

The name we give him comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Mexica. Mictlantecuhtli is formed from Mictlán, “the place of the dead,” and tecuhtli, “lord”: the lord of the place of the dead. You have already seen that root: Mitla, in Oaxaca, owes its name to Mictlán, as I told you in front of the [stone mosaics](mna_s07_grecas_mitla). But note this: this altar is several centuries older than the Mexica. We do not know what this figure was called by those who modeled it; it is called this because it is the name we know from the chronicles. It is a label of today on a much older image.

According to those chronicles, ordinary dead people made a journey of four years to Mictlán, where Mictlantecuhtli reigned with his companion, Mictecacíhuatl, “the lady of Mictlán.” Further on, in the West Mexico Hall, you will see the dog that, according to those same beliefs, helped the dead cross the last river. Here the image is of the master of the final destination: the one who waits at the end of the road.

Look at the material, even though it is a replica. Unfired clay is modeled like that of a vessel, but it does not go through fire: it dries, it is painted, and there it stays. That explains its fragility: a raw clay figure is exactly the kind of work that time tends to erase. It is thought to have reached us because the earth covered it and protected it for centuries.

A curious fact for later: the Mexica also made life-size clay figures of this same god. They have been found at the Templo Mayor, next to the Zócalo, and are displayed in the site museum. So this image of death, so ancient on the Gulf, stayed alive centuries later in the heart of the empire.

Death had many faces in Mesoamerica. In the Maya Hall, nine stucco gods watch over a king’s sleep in his tomb. And on the upper floors, in the hall of the Huastec and the Totonac, you will see how the dead are remembered today with arches of flowers and feasts. From the lord of death to the festival of the dead, there is a thread of more than a thousand years.

Before you return to the display cases, do not take away a gloomy idea. This image was not made to frighten for its own sake, but to give a place to the inevitable. And whoever gives death a place understands it a little better.

texto: Look for the human skulls that form part of the headdress
Look at the body: what makes it look almost like a skeleton?
Find the throne on which he is seated

texto.Material: Painted raw clay (the original); what is on display is a replica

texto.pregunta: Myth: This is the original sculpture of the god of death from El Zapotal.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a replica. The original, made of raw clay, is very fragile and is kept at the site, in El Zapotal, Veracruz.
